utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminary matters to be raised, which means that we could start the examination of the next witness which is Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, perhaps I might deal with a request to add three exhibits to the witness's 65 ter -- to the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list. Two of those exhibits were the subject of a filing made in June and the third exhibit is a CV of Mr. Curtis that we're seeking to add to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to any of the three for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any of the three. Could you list the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first one is 29111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The second is that 29112 and the third one 29113?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then leave is granted to add them to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Curtis, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Curtis. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could you please states your full name.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. Timothy Joseph Curtis, last name is spelled C-u-r-t-i-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see you've brought some materials into the courtroom. Could you just tell us what those are, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a copy of my report, an envelope with two photographs, and a copy of the -- a submission 5 or request number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Curtis, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I currently am the chief operations officer for laboratory services for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how long have you been the chief operations officer?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Since May of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And before then what was your profession?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I was also with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives but as the chief of their National Integrated Ballistic Identification Network. The NIBIN programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the ATF is, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The ATF is the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. It's a part of the United States Department of Justice, one of the bureaus, and their primary function of -- for the laboratories is to examine the forensic evidence recovered in arsons, bombings, and shooting cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned the NIBIN programme. Could you tell the Court what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, the NIBIN programme, National Integrated Ballistic Information Network, is a programme run throughout the United States in which they use the IBIS systems which are the integrated ballistic integrated systems. They are ballistic computers. And the NIBIN programme --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down a bit for the interpreters and the transcribers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. Yes, the NIBIN programme is part of the bureau's ballistic imaging programme where it links all the ballistic computers throughout the United States into a -- several different computer databases where they can be searched locally or nationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can just interject, I apologise, but I just received a note that my client requires to have a break to use the facilities. So if he can be permitted to attend to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic would like to withdraw from the courtroom for a moment or? Leave is granted. Any estimate as -- I mean, should we take a break? Can we continue meanwhile? Or what's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told five minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are we supposed to continue or would Mr. Mladic prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We can continue in his absence. And the Chamber understands this as an explicit waiver of his right to be present in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, you mention there the IBIS system, could you just give us a few lines about what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. The IBIS system is a computerised network that will take digital images of the digital photographs of the cartridge case, breechface, firing pin, and ejector marks. It also -- you can take images of fired bullets, and they are put into a database and they are searched using an algorithm [Realtime transcript read in error "algor ethnic"]. After the search results came back, and they are looked at by the IBIS specialist to determine if there are any high confidence matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned a cartridge case. Could you just provide details about what a cartridge case is? Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. A cartridge case is a part of the whole cartridge. A complete cartridge is a round of ammunition which has the case filled with gun powder, a bullet on the other end of it, and on the head portion there is a primer. When the cartridge is placed into a fire-arm, the -- and the trigger is pulled, the firing pin will strike the primer on the head of the case, that will detonate, igniting the gun powder. Once the gun powder is ignited it burns forming a gas. The gas pushes the bullet out of the barrel. It also helps push the breech where the bolt of the fire-arm rearwards extracting the case which is now fired and empty out of the fire-arm and ejecting it onto the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is it correct to also refer to a cartridge case as a shell case? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 29113 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. You said that they are searched using an algorithm. If I say -- it says "algor ethnic," but that apparently is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Algorithm, does that mean that the characteristics of the material which is examined is -- is reduced to a numerical set of data and then compared with others? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. It becomes digitalised and then numeric formulas and then it is searched that way. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, do you recall providing a copy of your CV to this Tribunal, to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the document on the screen now before you?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I do. It is a copy of my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Does it detail your education, professional training, and professional experience?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I note from your CV that you have testified over 125 times as an expert in firearms in US courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29113 receives number P1816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, has the ATF previously provided a report relating to analysis of certain cartridge cases to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 04613 [Realtime transcript read in error "01613"] to our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 4613, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's an ATF, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, laboratory report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you briefly just provide an overview of what this report is about?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. It's evidence that was received in our laboratory, both in November of 1997 and February of 1999. The first several pages, nine pages, list the exhibits, and then the following pages, 9 through 14, will list the results of those comparisons of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 15 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, do you see your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were you involved in the preparation of this report and the underlying investigation and that culminated in the production of this report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see you're listed as a fire-arms tool-mark examiner. Can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. Back in 2000, I was a fire-arm and tool-mark examiner with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, ATF for short. And as fire-arm examiner, my duties were to do the microscopic comparison of bullets, cartridge cases, or shell casings, and function testing of firearms. And the main purpose of doing these microscopic comparisons is to determine if the cartridge cases or bullets were fired from the same fire-arm or from a particular fire-arm if you have the fire-arm to examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you explain what it was that the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal asked the ATF to do in connection with this report and the cartridge casings they provided to you?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. They asked us to enter these into our IBIS system and then do a physical comparison of any possible matches that may have come up in the IBIS system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was the basic aim of that analysis? What was it to determine?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: To determine if any of these cartridge cases that were submitted had been fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put on the record that Mr. Mladic has returned to the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how were you able to make that determination as to whether these cartridge cases had been fired in the same fire-arm?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: In this case we received a list of request from our IBIS specialist who had entered the cartridge cases into the IBIS system, done their correlations and reviewed them. So they gave us a list of possible matches. And then as firearms examiners, we took the actual evidence items, and using a comparison microscope, which is two microscopes with a common eye piece, we were able to compare two cartridge cases at the same time and overlay the images of the cartridge cases in the microscope to see which markings are reproducing from one cartridge case to the next, and that's what we did in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now you mentioned that you received a list of requests from your IBIS specialist?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please go to 65 ter 29111.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, can you tell us what we're looking at here, if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of the list or the request that I received, request number 5, to inter-compare the exhibits that are in the left-hand column to the exhibits that are in the right-hand column to determine if they were fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So these shell casings are the result of the preliminary IBIS analysis and they identify the potential matching shell cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what the IBIS personnel thought were high confidence matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see a reference in this request to Zeleni Jadar and Kravica warehouse. Did you -- did those names mean anything to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in respect to the -- the potential matches identified the high confidence candidates, what would -- what would happen to those once they had been supplied to you by the IBIS examiners? What was the next step?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: The next step was for me to take the actual physical items, the cartridge cases, and compare them on the comparison microscope to determine if they were fired in the same fire-arm or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see on this memorandum there are some manuscript markings on the right side. Can you tell us what those are, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. They are markings I placed there during my examination of these items, such as in Exhibit 1627-10 when I compared it to Exhibit 0913-19. I wrote next to it "negative," that I was not able to identify those two cartridge cases as being fired in the same fire-arm. And then as you come down there are several other negatives, and there is one LSM, which is "lacks sufficient marks." In that case there were some markings there to indicate they may have been fired, but I did not have enough to positively say they were fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is it also that you couldn't say that they were not fired from the same fire-arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes it a special category against the negatives and the positives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on that page, Mr. Curtis?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Is that the signature on the right side?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the bottom right-hand side with the date of 1-20-00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And there is also a signature of a second person on that page. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is the signature of my supervisor, and he signed that when he received the request from the IBIS specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So of the potential matches identified in this particular memorandum, there are only two positive matches that you were able to make; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did you photograph the matches that you were able to make?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question. I see the second positive, there doesn't seem to be anything that 0913-47 is compared with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left-hand column under Exhibit 1627-55, it has the digital marks below it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could I tender this document as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2911 receives number P1817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have an additional question in relation to the signatures. Is it common in your system that first the supervisor signs a document and then you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was signing for receipt of the document from our IBIS specialist in this case, and for these -- the cases for this examination, yes, he would sign for them first. And then after I did my examination, he would -- I would sign my results. And after we did our report, after I signed my report, he would also review it and sign it after me in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Staying with that question, if you made a positive match, would that be verified by another member of your team?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. All of our matches and non-matches are verified by a second fire-arm -- qualified fire-arms examiner, as was in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You mention that you photographed these matches. What was the purpose of photographing of the matching of the shell cartridges?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Photographs, at the time we were doing them, just for our recollection later on to refresh our memory as to exactly what we saw under the microscope at that time so that later on if we have to go to court we have a documented photograph of what we had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the process of determining whether two cartridge cases match, would that be based on the photograph or what you saw through the microscope?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: All our identifications are through the microscope. We do not make identifications off photographs or off the IBIS computer screens. And when our second examiner confirms our verifications, they are also doing that through the comparison microscope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask you whether the image that you saw on the comparative microscope, whether that will be photographed again or stored in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can -- if we had the items of evidence and put them on a comparison microscope today, we can rephotograph them as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not at the time, if I ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You compared the items under the comparative microscope. I asked you whether you then photographed the image which would be visible and then you said: "It can -- if we had the items of evidence and put them on a comparison microphone scope today, we can rephotograph them as well." But were they photographed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I'm sorry, sir. We photographed all our positive results. We did not photograph any of the negative results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they are still stored and available, if need be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I actually brought those two photographs with me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll look at one of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- now, please. 65 ter 29112. Could we rotate that 180 degrees, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, could you please tell us what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. In this photograph we're looking at two different cartridge cases with the images overlaid. On the left-hand side is exhibit number 1627-55, and on the right-hand side is Exhibit 0913-89. In the area that is of significance in this photograph is on the right -- lower right-hand side at about 4.00 position on a clock, that would be the ejector mark on the cartridge cases. You can see a fine thin line coming down through the photograph, that is the hairline that is within the comparison microscope, and that separates the cartridge case on the left from the cartridge case on the right, and I'm able to sweep that line back and forth on the microscope to show those marks carry over from the one cartridge case to the other, thus identifying them as being fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to 4.00. Shouldn't we turn it 180 degrees in order to have it really at 4.00 or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On mine, it's on the lower right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On mine, it may be -- oh, it's turned already. I had it on my own screen. Yes. I see. Problem resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Curtis, is this one of the matching shell casing identified in request 5 that we looked at a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see the writing "request 5" on the left side and the date and some initials. Whose initials are those?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: They are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see "1.5 x" on the bottom of the screen, "1.5 x." What does that mean, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That means this photograph was taken at 15 times the resolution of the original size of the cartridge case, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, if I look at this picture - and could we still have the previous once - do I well understand that what is found at approximately 2.00 that where, of course, the -- what looks like a V but then horizontally, that that doesn't match because the cartridge may be put in the weapon in whatever position and, therefore, only marking made once the weapon is in position will match, whereas any other letters or whatever is -- may not match at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once the cartridge is put in the fire-arm, they can be put in at any position, and that horizontal V is actually part of the manufacturing head stamp on the cartridge case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which may or may not well be found on the other part as well if manufactured by the same factory but does not have to match if you compare the two because the only relevant matter is the marking made by the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next picture, please. Page 2. If we can rotate it so the 1627-55 is horizontal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Curtis, if you could tell us what we're looking at here, please?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Exhibit 1627-55, comparing it to Exhibit 0913-47. Once again, two fired cartridge cases; one on the left, and one on the right. And once again down around the 4.00 position. We're looking at the markings from the ejector of a fire-arm that are imparted to the case, and there is the hairline down through there, and if we sweep the hairline, the microscopic markings would once again -- they all line up indicating these two cartridge cases were fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Were the cartridge cases that you looked at the same calibre or a different calibre?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: They were the same calibre. They were all of the 7.62 by .39 calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is there a particular weapon that would discharge shell casings of that calibre?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Commonly the AK style of fire-arm. It fires the 7.62 by .39.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the matching shell casings in this picture, are those the second match that we looked at in request number 5, the second of the two matches?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29112 receives number P1818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 04613, please. That's the ATF report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Curtis, we have the ATF report before us. I see there is a subheading "Exhibits" and then there is a list of cartridge casings that goes on for the next nine pages in the report. What are those?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Those are the exhibits that were entered into our IBIS system that came back as a possible high confidence match to another exhibit. And there is a, I believe, eight and a half or nine pages of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if a cartridge casing was entered into the IBIS system and it came back with a negative match, would it be included in this list?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 9 of this document, please. Mr. Curtis, half way down the page we see the results of examination which states: "Microscopic examination of the above-listed cartridge case exhibits have been conducted. Based upon that examination, the following cartridge cases have been identified as having been fired in the same fire-arms." And then there is a list of cartridge casings identified with other cartridge casings. Can you just briefly explain this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. The cartridge case in the left-hand column would be identified as being fired in the same fire-arm as the cartridge case in the right-hand column directly opposite it -- opposite of it. And it's not saying that there was only one fire-arm, but those cartridge cases -- as example 1488/A1-3 and in the right-hand column 1486/332-1 were positively identified as being fired in the same fire-arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So when we looked at the memorandum number 5 earlier and you identified two matching shell cases, they would be included in these results?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 15 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, here we see your name and signature and the name of three other persons and their signatures. Can you tell us the role that those three other persons played in the investigation and preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. Three of us were fire-arm examiners: Myself, Mr. Danridge and Mr. Ols. And the three of us did the actual physical comparisons of the cartridge cases using the comparison microscopes to identify or eliminate cartridge cases being fired in the same fire-arms. Mr. Wilson, who is on the lower right, he was our section supervisor at the time and his role was basically to review our paperwork and make sure it was proper following all of our procedures. And afterwards, after we'd signed off on everything and he saw it was correct, he would then sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And as an example in respect of the two matches we identified for request number 5, do you know who it was that verified your own findings that there had been a match?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Walter Danridge verified my positive identification on those two identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And how do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: After I verified it, I asked Mr. Danridge to look into the microscope. He came to the same conclusion as I did. I took a photograph, marked the front of it as you had seen, but on the backside Mr. Danridge initialled and dated the photograph to verify that he agreed with my findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. Would Mr. Wilson also look at the photographs or just at the -- if I could say so, the procedural paperwork?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some instances he would look at the photographs, but he was more interested in the paperwork and us following proper procedures as far as the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The methods of analysis employed by the ATF, both the IBIS preliminary analysis phase and the microscopic analysis phase, were they consistent with -- or are they consistent with prevailing industry standards?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. The procedures we used back in 2000 are basically the same procedures that are followed today as far as comparisons of evidence on comparison microscope and working with the IBIS system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender that report. However, the English report, the last three pages of it comprises an information report prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, that's different to the report that the ATF prepared, and I would propose to redact those last three pages before the report is fully admitted. The reason I've not done that redaction now is because the report was filed in this form pursuant to the 94 bis procedure. If we can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I can have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you are talking about the last three pages. The last three pages follow the page we look at at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And those are an OTP information report that's actually already in evidence as P01733. So to ensure there is no confusion, I would propose redacting those from this particular report because it's a work product of the OTP rather than the ATF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to either suggestion, so at Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll assign an exhibit number to it and leave is already granted to have the last three pages of the reports, that's

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: replace the original one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Would it be better to remove them, Your Honour, or redact them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Removing is a way of redacting. I think if they do not appear at all in the B/C/S version and if they are more or less separate following the signature page, that removal would be acceptable as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. But we still need a number. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04613 receives number P1819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Curtis, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Mladic Defence team and you find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now before we begin with the actual questions, I do have to remind you, since we both will be speaking English, to please observe a pause between my question and your answer so as to permit the court reporters and translators to their job. Is that okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to begin. And to do so I'd like to turn to your CV which has now been admitted as P1816 in e-court. And if we can look at page 3 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S. And, sir, at the bottom we have the court qualifications that you testified about in direct. And by my count, it's 127 times. But without getting caught up in the actual total number, would you tell us out of those total times that you were an expert in other proceedings, how many of those times did you testify as to an examination of spent gun cartridge casings to try to match them up with other spent cartridge casings?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I cannot give an exact number, sir, but a majority of them -- because with the second bullet point where there is 118 testimonies, at that time I was a fire-arms examiner and police officer in Washington DC, and in that time-period there were a lot of shooting cases in the city, many of them involved either cartridge casings and/or bullets. So I would have to say a majority of those would compare cartridge cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Now if you have only one cartridge in a fire-arm, you would make shots with that fire-arm and then again compare the shell casings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to identify whether a cartridge matches with a weapon would take an intermediary step of producing another cartridge and then compare them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to that extent, at least in this respect, there seems to be no major difference because what you're still doing at the end is to compare cartridges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the approximately 127 times that you were an expert, how many of those times were in your capacity as an officer of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Sir, let's see. If you could scroll the page up, please, to the next -- the other way, please. It appears six of those testimonies were with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now in relation to all of these court appearances as an expert witness, have you been a court or defence expert or have you always been an expert testifying as a witness for the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I've testified for both the prosecution and the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you: Did you also have occasion in this -- in this case to perform testing on rounds that were test fired from weapons that were seized from the Army of Republika Srpska to see if they could be matched to any of those that are the subject of the report that has been entered into evidence today?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I do not know, sir. If they're on this list of request number 5, yes, I did, but other than that I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. A former Prosecution investigator, Dean Manning, who is an Australian law enforcement official, testified at this trial that in 1998 he participated in a mission to seize somewhere between 1.000 to 2.500 rifles from the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades of the VRS to test fire these rifles, and then that the investigation compared those spent rounds and casings to those which had been recovered at the graves, and that the results of those tests were a negative match. Do you know if your office did that work trying to match the spent cartridges to those recovered from the grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now looking at your CV on this same page that we have up in e-court, I see or note that you are a member of the AFTE, Association of Firearm and Tool Mark Engineers [sic]. Are you also a member of the IAI, the International Association of Identification?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, I am not a member of the IAI.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about the ENFSI, the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes. Are you an accredited member of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a few moments now to go over some AFTE issues with you. I take it, sir, that you are familiar with the AFTE criteria for identification committee?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the AFTE criteria for identification committee has promulgated that an identification means: "The likelihood another tool could have made the mark is so remote as to be considered a practical impossibility"?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that based on the AFTE theory of identification, there are four categories of examination outcomes which are also called "range of conclusions possible when comparing tool-marks," which are typically used by fire-arms examiners in the microscopic comparisons of cartridge casings and shot-shell casings?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to agree, then, that the first of these AFTE definitions is identification defined by the AFTE glossary as: "Agreement of a combination of individual characteristics and all discernible class characteristics where the extent of agreement exceeds that which can occur in the comparison of tool- marks made by different tools and is consistent with the agreement demonstrated by tool-marks known to have been produced by the same tool."

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I would agree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the second of the AFTE range of conclusions possible from an examination of a fire-arm is known as elimination which is defined as: "Significant disagreement of discernible class characteristics and/or individual characteristics."

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I agree with that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that the third possible range of conclusion as defined by the AFTE is known as inconclusive defined as either: "Some agreement of individual characteristics and all discernible class characteristics but insufficient for an identification," or, "agreement of all discernible class characteristics without agreement or disagreement of individual characteristics due to an absence in sufficiency or lack of reproducibility," or, "agreement of all discernible class characteristics and disagreement of individual characteristics but insufficient for elimination."

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to finish up those AFTE range of conclusions, the fourth would be unsuitable for microscopic comparison. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the tests that were conducted by your bureau on the spent bullet cartridge casings that are the subject of these reports conducted and accord with these AFTE identification and range of conclusion parameters that we have just gone through?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. Our cartridge case examinations were in compliance with these AFTE accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now is it correct, sir, that some differences always exist between cartridges that even are fired from the same gun?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: There are possibilities of differences. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would be a suitable moment for you to interrupt your cross-examination, then we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break of 20 minutes and would like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to talk with you about some general concepts that are paramount to your line of work to see if I am understanding them correctly. Now, first of all, am I correct that the marks which identify the gross properties of a fire-arm including but not limited to calibre, number of lands, number of grooves, direction of rifling twist, would be considered that fire-arm's class characteristics which are the marks that often are visible to the naked eye and that these class characteristics will be the same for any bullet or cartridge fired from any fire-arm of the same make and model and sometimes even several makes and models of the same manufacturer?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that as to class characteristics there exist reference works or resources that list these class characteristics for each fire-arm a particular manufacturer makes which would enable an examiner such as yourself to determine the type of fire-arm by examining the classes characteristics of either a recovered cartridge case or a recovered bullet?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: In my instances there are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if any reference manuals listing any class characteristics were utilised in this case to identify what would be the source of those spent cartridge casings so as to identify class characteristics of that type of fire-arm so that one could be aware of them when doing the review and comparison?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: None that I know of, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now would you agree that fire-arms identification, as a line of inquiry, assumes also that there are individual characteristics which would be unique and consistent to one specific fire-arm because in theory it is not possible to make two machined surfaces that are microscopically identical?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. There are the individual characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then would you agree in your line of work that one must be conscious of class characteristics, that they need to be known so as to be ruled out as being identified as individual characteristics because they can often times be mistaken for individual characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Well, the class characteristics will basically get us into the ballpark, but it's looking at the individual characteristics that will get us to the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that, but my question was more related towards knowing that a particular mark is a class characteristic of a particular run, manufacturing running of fire-arms, would be necessary so as to exclude those class characteristics from being mistakenly identified as individual characteristics of a specific fire-arm. Would you not agree?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if no reference manuals listing class characteristics were consulted for purposes of this review for which we have a report now, how can we exclude class characteristics from being identified as individual or accidental characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: In our examination of these cartridge cases, we looked at class characteristics even though we did not refer to a manual on class characteristics, and the class characteristics we did look at were the general shape of the firing pin impression, the basic lack of breechface markings on the head of the cartridge case, and general shape of the ejector marks. Those are the class characteristics. The individual characteristics that we then further looked at -- yeah, once we aligned all these other class characteristics were the individual markings within each of those class areas such as firing pin, breechface, and ejector mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I also want to talk with you about what's called subclass characteristics. Am I correct that those would be markings caused by temporary conditions in the manufacturing process such as a chipped or broken tool and, therefore, are the same on many fire-arms in a given production run although they would not be a permanent feature of the same class of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, there are those markings as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thus, sir, an examiner such as yourself must also decide if a mark that you see is an individual mark unique to a specific fire-arm or a potential subclass mark which may be shared by many fire-arms that were produced as part of the same production run. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the report that we have looked at in this case -- I guess there's two. There is the request number 5 and there is the more lengthy 15-page report that your bureau prepared for the Office of the Prosecutor. Do the reports prepared by your office identify what the class or subclass characteristics are that were identified for these cartridges such that they could be distinguished from and excluded as being individual characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: On a -- request number 5, all that we noted were if it was a negative identification or a positive or if it lacked sufficient markings for an identification to say negative or positive. We did not do complete work-sheets that would take into account all the other general class characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the normal everyday functioning of your lab for other cases, would such full work-sheets have been completed?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the work done in this case for the Office of the Prosecutor was not in full accord with the standard procedure that would have been followed by your office at the bureau for any other case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct. For this case, the items were first entered into the IBIS system, and the IBIS system was used to come up with the possible high confidence candidates. And it was from those list of high confidence candidates that we had -- did our actual microscopic comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the IBIS system in a second. I want to ask just a few more questions about the type of work that's normally done. Is it correct that some labs have in recent years instituted policies that identifications cannot be reached unless the suspect fire-arm is examined precisely to eliminate the possibility of subclass characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I'm not absolute about that one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And also when examining spent ammunition, whether the bullet or the -- actually, it would be on the casing, are there also what is called proof markings which would designate a country of origin of a particular munition?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: On the cartridge case there is the head stamp which normally determines the manufacturer of the ammunition, and -- but it does not specifically have to say which country it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were any head stamps or proof markings reviewed or investigated for purposes of your investigation in this case to determine the origin of the ammunition that was being reviewed?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, thus far we've been talking about fire-arms that were produced in the traditional factory milling process and the distinctions that would result in the components when they were milled at the factory. Am I also correct that when talking about modern fire-arms, there are also now some nowadays that are cast or stamped rather than being tool milled and that those that are cast or stampeded can have components that have the same markings and thus can have fire-arms that have identical individual markings as well?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Even a cast and stamped fire-arms, a majority of those or their parts do have some machining processes or processes done after the stamping to rid them of burrs that are on the surfaces so that they will also develop individual characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any work done in this particular case to determine if the fire-arms that were used to fire the cartridges that your bureau reviewed, whether those came from milled fire-arms or fire-arms that have been created with a casting or stamping process?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I did -- I'm sorry. I did not do any of that examination to look at fire-arms. I did not have a fire-arm to examine for request number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, in one of your previous questions where you were talking about "there are also now some nowadays that are cast or stamped," could you either -- could you clarify with the witness or press more -- be more precise in your question what you understand by "nowadays." These cast or stamped ones, they are produced since when if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, sir. I believe it's after the 1960s but I am not positive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But still before 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now ask you a few questions about the IBIS system that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can first of all look at P1818 together. P1819, I apologise. Thank you. And if we can turn to page 9 of the same, I believe that's where the actual results of the examination are specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to request number 5, it was very clear the role that the IBIS examination played in that report. Here we have discussion of the cartridges being microscopically examined. For purposes of this report, can you tell us how we can tell from the report which ones would have resulted from being identified by the use of the IBIS system as opposed to being identified pursuant to a microscopic review of an examiner or perhaps in addition to being identified pursuant to microscopic review of an examiner.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: The exhibits on pages 1 through 9 were all examined through the IBIS system, and they came up as possible high confidence matches to another cartridge case. And then as we got the separate request, in this case request number 5, I looked at the exhibits from request number 5, and that is the report I received from the IBIS examiner. And I did the microscopic comparison of those casings at that point. But before that, it was done by the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to the results and the review of the items on pages 9 through 15 of this report that we have in the system now, did you perform the microscopic examination and analysis of all of these or were there colleagues involved?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: There were colleagues involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was your work limited to doing the microscopic examination or of -- of a certain number of these items, or did you also participate in the verification of items that your colleagues either identified or excluded?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I also participated in the verification of items that my colleagues identified or excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any way of knowing what percentage or what portion of these would have been ones that you verified as opposed to ones that you were the primary opinion on?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, just so that we are clear, we have been talking about the IBIS system, and I want to know: Are you referring to the older identification system manufactured by Forensic Technologies WAI, Inc. of Canada or some of the newer modifications such as IBIS 3.0 or the newer brass tracks CD system. Which IBIS was it that was used for purposes of preparing this report and identifying these cartridge casings?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: In 1999 and 2000, they only had the older version, the original IBIS system which is known to us as the heritage system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you there a question. The IBIS system, if I understand you well, is primarily used to make selection of those cartridges which deserve to be further examined microscopically by a person. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. In this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So any shortcomings in the IBIS system as far as positive results are concerned would be immediately corrected by the comparative microscopical review on the materials. Negatives is something different, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Any positive results would be verified then by the fire-arms examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in the IBIS system would have been -- well, whether wrong or not, identified the cartridges as, I think you said, "confidence," well, at least as good candidates for a match, that would result in a negative outcome of the microscopical examination of those -- of that material, whereas if the IBIS system would not classify them as good candidates, you most likely would never find out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to other work that your office at the bureau would do for other similar cases, would it not also be part of the normal procedure to compare the actual bullets that were recovered from a scene using the FBI's general rifling characterise or GRC file which is organised by number of calibre, number of lands and grooves, direction or twists, widths of lands and grooves, and other categories?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: If we had bullets, we would measure the lands and grooves and compare them to the general rifle and characteristics database, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if in this case you were advised of the existence of bullets that had been recovered?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If your bureau had received bullets to be analysed, am I safe in assuming that either you or the other two individuals who signed this report -- or actually three individuals that signed this report would be aware of that process?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: One of the three of us may have been, but I was not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now in relation to the IBIS system and -- well, first of all, I presume that you have knowledge of the test performed on that system known as AB 1717 in relation to California's consideration of whether or not to implement that system in their jurisdiction. Do you -- are you familiar with that particular study?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I remember hearing of the study. I don't recall exactly what it was at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we talk about other studies, I think we can step away from IBIS for a moment since we've, I think, talked about the possibility of errors and how those are then rectified by the microscopic evaluation, but are you familiar with the 1955 study performed by Alfred Biasotti which found that 15 to 20 per cent of the stria and bullets fired from different .38 special Smith & Wesson fire-arms matched. Are you familiar with that study, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And have I accurately summarised the results of that particular study according to your recollection of the same?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I believe he also went on to say that you could have consecutively matching stria totalling, I believe, it was six to nine impressions, and that's all you would need for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the 1997 study by Joseph J. Masson based on the IBIS system which found that increasing similarities were being discovered in the individual characteristics of tool-marks on ammunition components known to have been fired by different guns of that calibre?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that Masson's study found that similarities between known non-matching tool-marks were sometimes so great that even under a comparison microscope it was difficult to tell the tool-marks apart and not erroneously attribute them to the same gun. Are you aware of that conclusion reached in that 1997 study?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to turn to the actual investigation that was done. And the first question I want to know is, am I correct that some of the spent cartridge casings were actually collected by and brought from Bosnia by ATF bureau staff, whereas other batches were brought and delivered by staff of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I am not sure who brought them in, sir. I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of the methods employed to secure these cartridges and keep them separated from one another?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Once they're brought in -- once they were brought into our laboratory, they were entered into the evidence vault until the examiner or the IBIS specialists working them signed for them and then they were in their custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say, "Once they were brought into our laboratory ...," can I take from that, sir, that your bureau would not be in a position to verify or opine as to what manner they were secured in prior to coming to your laboratory, except, perhaps, for the once instance where cartridges may have been brought by a member of your staff?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I cannot say how they were kept prior to our receiving them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to this particular case, is this one that you would consider a high profile case for your office?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any instruction or a concern to obtain results as promptly and quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, sir. It's just a -- as they got entered into the IBIS and they were evaluated, after evaluation then they were assigned to a fire-arms examiner for comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you've already told us earlier that the procedure for filling out work-sheets was not followed in full for this review. What I'd like to know now is if there were any other protocols or procedures which your office would normally employ that were not complied with in relation to the review and investigation done in this case?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, just the fire-arm examiner work-sheets were the only forms that were not followed. And during the -- as well as entering the items into IBIS prior to the fire-arms examiner looking at them, that was a different set in protocols. Normally the fire-arms examiner examines the items first and then gives them to the IBIS specialist to enter, but in this case we had the IBIS machine doing the portion of the work for us to narrow it down our microscopic examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you allow me one clarifying question. What would these fire-arm examiner work-sheets tell us if they are full? What kind of information is there contained in those work-sheets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a cartridge case, the -- it would have the exhibit number, the possible brand, manufacturer of the cartridge case, and any general characteristics on that cartridge case, shape of the firing pin, if there were breechface markings, if there were parallel, cross-hatch, granular, and then basically our conclusion from examining that one cartridge case to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now that kind of information, could that still be obtained on the basis of the shell casings which have been preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it can. And I believe the IBIS personnel did partial work-sheets, so it may be on their work-sheet as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think, for the record, we have not received any partial work-sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the IBIS personnel actually did have partial work-sheets? Are you -- is that a confident memory, or are you just speculating, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, we did receive some IBIS work-sheets from the ATF and those have all been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you need the assistance, I take it that Mr. Jeremy will help you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with -- with respect to the normal procedure of examining all the casings that were to come into your office in preparing your work-sheet, wouldn't that also assist the examiner in determining potential class characteristics that should be excluded from the further review and in terms of not being misidentified as individual characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Well, by looking at the cartridge cases, you can determine through the microscope what the class characteristics are, such as the shapes of the firing pin impressions and the breechface and the ejector markings. So in a sense we did that examination in our mind's eye through the microscope but we just did not note it on our work-sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But the examination you would have done in your mind's eye that was not on the work-sheet would have only been for a smaller subset of the cartridges; i.e., those for which the IBIS had already given a high probability of match; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were any interim reports or bench notes maintained as part of the review that your office performed for this case?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Not that I know of, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be a normal part of your work, procedure, and practice within the laboratory to maintain interim reports or bench notes?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Can you define interim reports for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, from my understanding of -- interim reports would be anything that pre-dates the final report that is signed by the examiners and by the supervisor.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If there is a draft report prepared, normally they are not preserved. It is the final report that is our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us the process of what happens between a draft report being prepared and a final report being generated? How -- how do -- how does -- who is in charge of creating the final report from the draft?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: In this case since there were three examiners on this case, Mr. Ols prepared the final report from the draft, and the only changes that may have been made to that without any of our knowledge may have been typographical errors that were corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now has the normal work and methodology utilised in your laboratory been the subject of any peer reviewed or blind testing?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at P1817, and I hope I have the number right. This should be the request number 5 memo report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have that in e-court, I'd have some questions for you on that document. Now, while looking at this document now, I'd first like to ask you about the information contained at the top. It comes from Randy Hartman to Ben Wilson. Am I correct that Mr. Hartman is not an employee of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is the company that Mr. Hartman is an employee of, Forensic Technology Inc., in fact, a subsidiary company of the Canadian manufacturer of the IBIS system?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now could you explain for us -- first of all, I assume that he is the IBIS specialist that you've been referring to for -- at least for request number 5?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: He is one of several, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would the subject cartridge casings that were secured in the ATF vault, would they have been given to the IBIS specialist at this outside company for purposes of inputting them into the IBIS system?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. We had four ATF IBIS specialists working within our laboratory doing the entries, and I do not know if Mr. Hartman was privy to those cartridge cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the identifications that are handwritten -- pardon me, withdraw that. The notes that are handwritten on the right-hand side of the document, sir, that you've identified as being positive, negative, and lacks sufficient marks, could you tell me, since we talked earlier about the AFTE guidelines and the ranges of conclusions that were possible resulting from an examination, why weren't the AFTE standard categories or terminology used for purposes of this review?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: For -- during my examination, negative is basically the same as the second category of the AFTE, Association of Firearm and Toolmark Examiners, range of conclusions. The "pos" [Realtime transcript read in error "pause"] is similar to the first one, where it was "positive identification," and then the "lacks sufficient marks" was with the third one. Just in making my rough notes, everyone in my office, we all used basically the same terminology knowing what we are referring to when we say "negative," "positive," or "lacks sufficient markings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a clarification of the transcript that might not get picked up when itself replayed. Transcript 44, line 12. The -- it currently reads "pause." I think the witness said "pos" as a shorthand for positive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is not a word often used and perhaps not easily recognised, "pos" being p-o-s and stands for positive result. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I also see -- I should have gone back to my prior method os spelling out the acronym. Just to make sure it's correctly recorded, it's A-F-T-E, AFTE, but it's A-F-T-E as the acronym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jeremy, everything of course became perfectly clear on page 44, line 16. There the negative, the positive, and the third category are mentioned as the three used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now this particular report as considerably more detailed information than the other report we looked at, the 15 pages. Would this report be an exemplar type of work or review that was undertaken for purposes of doing the identifications -- or confirming the identifications, I should say, that are reflected in the longer 15-page report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: This request number 5 with the notations on it were -- basically are notes for this and they would be used for preparing the longer report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so when we earlier talked about bench notes or interim reports, would such a document as this memo with your handwritten modifications qualify as a bench note or interim report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I stand corrected on that. This would be considered a bench note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the -- you say it's considerably more detailed. Are you talking about the tables or are you talking about the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the tables, as far as I can see them -- and perhaps the witness could help us out. What we see is that in the long list, all the negatives and all the insufficient material or insufficient markings are left out - that's the quintessence of that report, at least where the matches are described - and apart from that, we only have exhibit numbers on what seems to be in this table to be one-in-the-same case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand exactly what we find in this table, what apparently we do not find in the other report. We looked at the 15 pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the first nine pages of the long report, you would have all the exhibit numbers listed that are on request number 5 because they were deemed by the machine as possible matches. But from page 9 through 14, you would only have the positive matches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that were verified by fire-arms examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So by -- the negatives are in -- and whatever other you could think of as to compare but did not match.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not written out in any detail further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: However, one difference is that here we can tell whoever did the microscopic examination, whereas on the long list we can't tell and you can't tell us right now which ones you did; right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: That's correct. Except for the ones I have note here we can find in the long list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
