utterances.text: Right. Now the question I have is if any drafts would have been destroyed as procedure why do we have request number 5, and does such is a document exist for any of the other cartridge casings that would have been reviewed and reported in the long report that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- again for the record, there are requests numbers 1 to 13. Those have been provided to the Defence and translated into the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Memos -- including memos such as this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Correct. So 5 is an example, and there are actually 13 of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I am just trying understand the witness's earlier answer that if such things would have been discarded, why were they saved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My draft report of the laboratory report itself, if there were typographical errors, would have been discarded and just the final report signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now I'm confused. I did understand from Mr. Jeremy, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that for all the other requests, all 13 similar documents, memos do exist and are disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'm still confused by your next question, Mr. Ivetic. You're trying to understand the witness's earlier answer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Previous answer today where he indicated that any interim reports or drafts would have been destroyed as a part of their procedure, and now he's, I think, clarified that these are not considered draft report. That a draft report would actually be the pre-proofing, I guess, version of the longer report that would need to be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood it like that from the beginning but then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can go to the next page of this exhibit -- no -- no. Then let's turn to P1818, which now should be the photographs of -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, are these what would be called photomicrographs in your line of work, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now can you explain for me why these photomicrographs are not of the entire circumference of the cartridge casing?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: This is photomicrograph was taken at what I have noted as 1.5 x which is actually 15 times the size of the head of the cartridge case, it's magnified, and the main area that I was concerned with here is the ejector marks that appear on the right-hand and left-hand cartridge cases that are in this photo at the 10.00 position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that normally the best and accepted procedure is to photograph the entire circumference so as to get all of the potential marks so as to identify or eliminate class markings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, sir, I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do photomicrographs that were taken of all the other cartridges which were positively identified or reviewed for purposes of your report all taken focusing on the part that matches most closely instead of the entire circumference of a shell casings breechface?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection that would be the case, but I have not reviewed all of those photographs in many years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a standing practice within your laboratory to only take photomicrographs of a particular section of a bullet casing as opposed to the entire circumference, or was that a decision that was made to do so in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: The taking of the photomicrographs in our laboratory, the procedures for it and policies, basically was so we would have something to refresh our recollection of the markings and the areas in which we made our identifications. It was not required to take the full circumference of the cartridge case but just the areas where we felt the identification is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when you are talking about the whole of the cartridge heading, are you talking about the big one or about the other part? I mean, you can't have the -- both? They would overlap if you had -- I mean, the whole system, the whole technique is to show a specific part of a shell casing, put it next to a similar part of another shell casing, and then see how any stria -- I don't know how you call it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stria are connecting. So therefore when you are talking about the whole of the shell case, certainly that could not be done for either of them because it would contradict the technique you are using. Therefore, I'm asking whether you would expect, for example, the -- more information from the -- from the one shell casing where we see -- it looks something like perhaps AK or at least at -- or what you meant by your question. I mean, if you take the whole of the shell case you can't overlay it any further with the portion of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand. And perhaps we should go to the second page of this exhibit where there are two separate shell cases as two separate photographs. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. But I didn't understand the question entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. In my version there is a page that has the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, am I correct that in addition to the work done in doing the overlays that photomicrographs were taken of each individual bullet that was being reviewed and being matched and identified as a positive match?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I don't believe photomicrographs of each cartridge case individually were done. They were not done by me in this case for request 5. And to get the whole head into the photograph, I would have had to go to a lower magnification and then I would not be able to see the area clearly enough where I had made my identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it not be standard procedure to first make a photomicrograph of the two shells with their full circumference, have those photomicrographs side by side and then do a second at higher magnification to discuss specific areas of either a -- for comparison purposes either of match or of exclusion of difference?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: It was not the policy of our laboratory to do that work, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jeremy, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, at transcript page 38 you were asked about methods to secure the shell casings. Were the shell casings categorised by the ATF? Were they marked in order to keep track of those?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. As the IBIS specialist recovered the shell casings from their evidence vault, they cleaned them and then they marked them with the exhibit number that they received them with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you've told us during the cross-examination that fire-arms examiner work-sheets were not produced. Now had they been reduced, could they have changed the conclusions that you reached in respect to which cartridge cases matched?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, they would not have changed the conclusions for the matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During cross-examination you were asked about class characteristics and individual characteristics and the risk of misinterpreting a class characteristic for an individual characteristic and therefore come to a conclusion based on a class characteristic rather than on individual characteristics, which would mean that the whole range of shell casings in that class would then be mistaken for identical ones where they were only from the same batch. Did you have ever in your career the experience that you had to reconsider your identification because you had misinterpreted what you later found to be a class characteristic where you initially thought of them as individual characteristics?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: No, sir. I have not had to reconsider it. And one of the reasons is we always have a second qualified examiner review our work and our identifications and non-identifications so that we are not making that mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything published about the risk of making such a mistake?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: I believe there are in the AFTE journals, which is the professional publication for the Association of Firearm and Toolmark Examiners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was the number of cartridges to be compared in this case uncommon, exceptional, or was it normal that you have so many even possible matches out of two series of cartridges that were provided to your laboratories?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CURTIS
utterances.text: This case was uncommon for our laboratory because of the number of cartridge cases to be examined, and that is why we altered our procedures to use the IBIS system to help narrow down the microscopic comparisons that we would have to do, the inner comparisons. And otherwise most of our cases have, say, 20 cartridge cases or fewer, and this one had up into the thousands, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any questions? Further?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Curtis, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and having explained to us the -- all these technical matters, more in general to have answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break. After the break we'll resume with the next witness who will testify in closed session, if I am well informed. Then we'll take the break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed that one of the parties would like to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Just a request. We said that we would cross-examine the witness whose due to arrive now for three and a half hours. Yesterday we said it would be less. And now I have a request and a proposal. We will cross-examine this witness for an hour and a half, but we kindly ask that part of this time be a bonus for cross-examining the expert who is due to arrive in two days since our assessment is that we will need somewhat more time, more than the two and a half hours we had originally said we would need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said the expert -- we have two experts still on our list, I think, for the remainder of the week. Any one of the two is special?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I don't think that there are any protective measures. I am speaking of Mr. Haglund. I think that it is all right for me to say his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think there is any problem with that. Well, the Chamber is usually not providing bonuses, but if you say whether or not the Chamber will also consider that you have saved time with this witness when you asked for more time, time in itself is not the relevant thing. Important is a relevant and focused cross-examination. And if you can't do that in the time you estimated, then the Chamber certainly will be more forthcoming even after you've saved time with the present witness. Is that an answer to your question, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, Your Honour. And we shall do our best for it to be that way and we will honour our time commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session to hear the evidence of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 23rd of July, in this same courtroom III at 9.30 in the morning.
